cues.text: A Convert of the Nahua People
Born around 1474 near Cuautitlán in the valley of Anáhuac, in what is now central Mexico, Juan Diego belonged to the indigenous Nahua people.
Known before his baptism by his Nahuatl name, Cuauhtlatoatzin, "singing eagle," he lived through the traumatic Spanish conquest of the Aztec empire as a young and middle-aged man.
Around 1524, together with his wife, he embraced the Christian faith brought by Franciscan missionaries.
He became known for a devotion so committed that he regularly walked long distances to receive religious instruction and attend Mass, even after he was widowed and living alone in his later years.
A Lady on Tepeyac Hill
On the morning of December 9, 1531, Juan Diego, by then a widower of about fifty-five, hurried across Tepeyac hill to hear Mass.
It celebrated the feast of the Immaculate Conception.
There, he encountered a young woman of radiant appearance who identified herself as the Mother of the true God.
She asked him to go to the bishop of Mexico City, Fray Juan de Zumárraga, requesting a temple be built on that very spot in her honor.
A Bishop's Understandable Doubt
Bishop Zumárraga, understandably cautious about an indigenous farmer's report of such an extraordinary vision, questioned Juan Diego closely and had him watched.

Ultimately, he asked for a sign before acting on the request—a reasonable demand from a churchman responsible for discerning genuine revelation from possible error or deception in a newly evangelized land.
Roses in December, and an Image Left Behind
The lady appeared to Juan Diego again on December 12, as he hurried past Tepeyac to fetch a priest for his gravely ill uncle.
She reassured him of his uncle's recovery and instructed him to gather flowers from the same hilltop.
Though it was winter and nothing should have been blooming, Juan Diego found fresh Castilian roses growing impossibly out of season.
Gathering these roses into his tilma , a simple cloak woven of coarse cactus fiber, Juan Diego carried them to the bishop as instructed.
When he unfolded the cloak before Zumárraga, the roses tumbled to the floor, and both men discovered a full-length image of the lady imprinted upon the coarse fabric itself.
The image remains, to this day, preserved in a manner that continues to defy straightforward scientific explanation, given the material’s fragility and the passage of nearly five centuries.
A Bridge Between Two Worlds
The image on Juan Diego's tilma depicted the Virgin with features and symbolism readily recognizable to indigenous Mexican eyes.
Historians of the period widely credit it with dramatically accelerating the conversion of Mexico's indigenous population in the years that followed.
This devotion offered, for the first time, a maternal image of the faith that indigenous converts could recognize as genuinely their own rather than simply imposed from a foreign culture.
Millions who had shown little interest in the missionaries' preaching came, within just a few years of the apparition, to seek baptism.
They did so at the very hill where Juan Diego had first met the lady he called, in his own Nahuatl tongue, by an affectionate name for Mother.
Legacy
Juan Diego spent the remaining years of his life as a humble caretaker of the chapel built at Tepeyac in fulfillment of Mary's request, dying there around 1548.
Beatified in 1990 and canonized in 2002 by Pope John Paul II, Juan Diego became the first indigenous saint of the Americas.
His tilma remains enshrined today at the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Mexico City, among the most visited Catholic shrines anywhere in the world.

It is a lasting monument to the single, humble morning encounter of an indigenous widower who simply happened to be hurrying to Mass, and whose obedience opened an entire continent's heart to the Gospel.
